title: Greene v. McElroy
lead: An aeronautical executive lost his clearance and livelihood after proceedings that concealed adverse sources. The Supreme Court resolved who had authorized those procedures, while expressly reserving their ultimate constitutionality.

actors.name: William Lewis Greene
actors.role: Aeronautical engineer and corporate executive whose lost clearance prevented continued work in his profession.

actors.name: Engineering and Research Corporation
actors.role: Military contractor known as ERCO; employed Greene until access restrictions made his position impossible.

actors.name: Defense and Navy officials
actors.role: Administered and reorganized industrial-clearance procedures and revoked Greene’s access.

actors.name: Industrial security boards and review office
actors.role: Administrative bodies that heard Greene but withheld confidential adverse sources.

proceedings: First review board restored Secret authorization in January 1952 after a 1951 revocation.
Navy revoked access in April 1953; new regional board upheld adverse action after April 1954 hearings; review office affirmed in March 1956.
District court granted government summary judgment and D.C. Circuit affirmed.
Supreme Court on June 29, 1959 reversed and remanded; five joined the opinion, three concurred only in judgment, and Clark dissented.
limits: Greene had hearings, but could not confront or cross-examine adverse sources. The Court found missing explicit authorization, not an unconditional entitlement to classified material, a final constitutional prohibition, a damages award, or a mandatory clearance. It reserved inherent presidential power and whether legislation was indispensable.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with complete effective canonical brief; no new independent full-opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Greene’s military-contract career depends on clearance
sections.cue: Why did exclusion from classified work threaten more than access to one room?
paragraphs: After aeronautical training, William Lewis Greene joined Engineering and Research Corporation (ERCO) in 1937 as a junior engineer and draftsman. He rose to vice president and general manager, working on products including a Navy flight simulator and rocket launcher. ERCO developed and manufactured armed-services equipment, and classified projects required cleared staff.

Greene received Confidential and Top Secret clearances in 1949 and 1950. ERCO’s security agreement required exclusion of designated people from areas containing military contract work and protection against unauthorized classified access. Although the agreement said exclusion did not necessarily require dismissal, Greene’s executive duties depended on access; that abstract distinction would not save his job.

sources.pinpoint: Career and clearances; 360 U.S. at 475–77 & nn.1–2

sections.title: The first adverse decision is reversed after a hearing without adverse witnesses
sections.cue: Which favorable decision preceded the later discharge?
paragraphs: In November 1951, the Army-Navy-Air Force Personnel Security Board warned ERCO that its facility clearance was threatened by a tentative adverse decision about Greene. The company vouched for his loyalty and discretion, but Greene took a furlough. In December the Board revoked clearance, citing alleged Communist associations, embassy contacts, and attendance at an asserted Communist-front dinner during 1943–1947.

Greene sought Industrial Employment Review Board review and appeared with counsel on January 23, 1952. He explained that many questioned individuals were his former wife’s associates, attributed some publications and activities to that marriage, rejected her views, denied Communist affiliation, and described embassy visits as attempts to sell ERCO products. Company executives and military officers corroborated him.

The government called no witnesses. Questions nevertheless revealed confidential investigative reports unavailable for Greene to inspect or test. On January 29, the review board reversed the adverse determination and authorized Secret work. That successful review was an earlier stage, not relief following the later job loss.

sources.pinpoint: First administrative process; 360 U.S. at 477–80 & nn.3–5

sections.title: Reorganization brings a renewed exclusion and discharge
sections.cue: What happened without a prior hearing in April 1953?
paragraphs: On March 27, 1953, the Defense Secretary abolished both boards and instructed military departments to establish regional boards with uniform procedures and standards; existing criteria remained during transition. On April 17, the Navy Secretary independently informed ERCO that Greene’s continued access was inconsistent with national security and requested exclusion from classified areas and information. That action had no preceding hearing.

An ERCO executive explained that Greene could not perform his position without access, leaving no choice but discharge and no other reason for dismissal. The Navy refused further discussion as useless. Greene’s later efforts to return to aeronautical engineering failed without clearance, and he worked instead as an architectural draftsman.

sections.title: The regional board hears Greene but conceals the sources
sections.cue: What did later administrative review establish and leave untested?
paragraphs: After reconsideration requests, the Eastern Industrial Personnel Security Board received the case. An April 9, 1954 letter gave thirteen general specifications nineteen days before a hearing beginning April 28 and continuing two additional days. They concerned Greene’s first marriage, publications, bookshop membership, radio-station investment, embassy business contacts, and acquaintances. These were allegations with contextual explanations, not Supreme Court findings of espionage or political belief.

The Board warned that its transcript would omit confidential investigations, informant identities, and source-revealing material. Greene answered extensive questions and produced corroborating witnesses, but could not confront adverse declarants or investigators. He testified that his prior salary was $18,000 and his current drafting pay $4,700; a separate affidavit gave an initial $4,400 figure. The Court viewed impairment of his profession as substantial.

The regional board upheld the adverse action without detailed findings, invoking security. Greene requested review in September 1955. In March 1956, the review office supplied general conclusions about associations and sympathies, questioned credibility and trustworthiness, and affirmed. Untrustworthiness had not previously been charged or found, as the opinion’s note observed. Those remained administrative determinations, not judicial findings of disloyalty.

sources.pinpoint: Regional process and final review; 360 U.S. at 483–90 & nn.14–19, 491 n.21

sections.title: Greene’s judicial challenge loses below but presents an authorization question
sections.cue: Why did the Supreme Court consider the injury reviewable?
paragraphs: After the 1954 regional decision, Greene sued in the District of Columbia for a declaration that revocation was unlawful, restraint against officials acting on it, and notice to ERCO that it was void. After final administrative review, both sides sought dispositive relief. The district court granted government summary judgment, and the D.C. Circuit affirmed.

The circuit acknowledged serious employment and reputational harm but treated clearance decisions as executive matters beyond judicial resolution and rejected confrontation and disclosure demands. Greene challenged both authorization and constitutionality, invoking private employment and pursuit of his profession. Government acknowledged the harm but called it incidental to protecting military secrets and defended confidentiality as necessary for information sources.

The Supreme Court accepted standing to challenge substantially harmful unauthorized official action. Chief Justice Warren chose the narrower authorization question: had Congress or the President authorized depriving Greene of private employment through factual determinations withholding confrontation and cross-examination? Departmental directives, rather than a specific statute or presidential order addressing those procedures, created the challenged program.

sources.pinpoint: Judicial proceedings and framing; 360 U.S. at 490–96 & nn.20–24

sections.title: Traditional safeguards make the departure a decision for politically responsible actors
sections.cue: What did the majority require express authorization to cover?
paragraphs: Warren explained why factual accusations producing serious consequences ordinarily require enough disclosure to expose error. Reports may reflect faulty memory, bias, mistaken inference, or malice. Here boards generally did not see informants and often did not question investigators. The notes illustrated subjective impressions about Greene’s marriage and politics and possibly multiple hearsay layers. Those concerns supported explicit authorization for the departure, without finally adjudicating every clearance procedure’s constitutional validity.

Executive Orders 10290 and 10501 regulated classification, transmission, and dissemination, including outside the Executive, but did not expressly permit deprivation of existing civilian employment and profession without an effective opportunity to challenge adverse evidence. Wartime Executive Order 8972 supplied no sufficiently specific authority either.

The National Security Act’s structure and general administrative powers, the Armed Services Procurement Act’s contracting provisions, and criminal laws protecting classified or cryptographic information demonstrated legitimate responsibilities without authorizing this procedure. Nor did appropriations ratify it. A particular appropriation concerned reimbursement for workers eventually cleared, and hearings did not adequately reveal the disputed procedure for deliberate approval. General funding for multifaceted agencies was also insufficient.

The majority accepted that delegation can often be inferred where power is clear and officials implement standards with political acquiescence. It had no difficulty recognizing authority for clearance with confrontation and cross-examination. But a serious departure from traditional fairness in a constitutionally doubtful area required Congress or the President consciously to take responsibility. Silence could not leave that choice to administrators by default.

sources.pinpoint: Safeguards and authority analysis; 360 U.S. at 496–508 & nn.25–31

sections.title: Three concurring Justices narrow their agreement; Clark sees adequate authority
sections.cue: Why did eight votes for reversal not endorse every majority passage?
paragraphs: Justices Frankfurter, Harlan, and Whittaker concurred only in the judgment because presidential or congressional authorization had not been demonstrated, expressly reserving validity. Harlan separately criticized constitutional discussion beyond that basis as premature and unnecessary. He also answered the suggestion that reversal required disclosure of secrets: nothing compelled classified access despite reliability concerns. The unresolved question was lawful procedure.

Justice Clark dissented. He denied a constitutional right to classified information and thought government procurement disclosure created no such right merely because private employment depended on it. He found the safeguards adequate and relied on confidentiality precedents while disputing Warren’s treatment of them.

Clark read wartime directives, departmental practice, the National Security Act, presidential reports, the 1953 reorganization, loyalty rules, congressional publication of regulations, and continued appropriations as ample approval. He rejected the majority’s demand for deliberate authorization of this particular departure. His predictions of litigation and wage-loss claims, and criticism that the constitutional discussion cast a wider cloud, were dissenting warnings rather than awards or holdings.

sources.pinpoint: Concurrences and dissent; 360 U.S. at 508–24 and Clark nn.1–12

sections.title: Reversal returns the case without directing unconditional clearance
paragraphs: On June 29, 1959, the Court reversed the D.C. Circuit and remanded to the district court. Five Justices joined Warren’s opinion, three agreed only with reversal, and Clark dissented. Officials lacked explicit congressional or presidential authorization for the procedure used to deprive Greene of his private employment.

The Court did not determine whether express authorization would make nonconfrontation constitutional, whether the President inherently could establish such a system, whether legislation was indispensable, or the ultimate limits on either branch. It ordered neither unconditional clearance nor a final wage award. Saying simply that Greene received no hearing would also be wrong: he had hearings but lacked confrontation and cross-examination of adverse sources. No later remand outcome or present clearance-law conclusion is supplied.
